SENCUT Sylor Review: You’ve Reviewed One Fifty Dollar Knife, You’ve Reviewed Them All

ByBlair Witkowski
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 9:46
Instaread

I bought the SENCUT Sylor with my own money because I wanted to see if the boring answer was still the right one.

Here’s what I mean. If you spend any time in the knife world, you already know the script for SENCUT and its big brother CIVIVI. Somebody posts a review, the comments say “oh look, another well built knife from SENCUT,” and everybody moves on. It’s become a running joke. And honestly, at this point in my life, I get it. Sometimes it feels like you’ve reviewed one fifty dollar knife, you’ve reviewed them all.

So back in July I picked up the gray G10 Sylor with the black DLC coated D2 blade, put it in my pocket, and paid attention.

It’s been about two months of real carry. It came along on a family vacation, and it was my daily knife the week I moved my daughter back into college, which is a week of cutting tape, zip ties, packing straps, and every kind of cardboard they make. That’s plenty of time to know whether a knife annoys you. This one doesn’t. It also didn’t make me fall in love. Both of those things are the review.

View on Amazon

What the Sylor Is

SENCUT is the budget line under the WE Knife umbrella, sitting below CIVIVI. Same factory discipline, cheaper materials, lower price. That’s the whole formula, and it’s why a SENCUT at forty bucks usually feels like it should cost a little more than the sticker.

The Sylor is a full size liner lock flipper with a clip point blade. It comes in gray, white, or red G10. Mine is the gray S25056-1 with the black DLC coated blade. Depending on where you buy, you’ll pay somewhere between forty and forty six dollars.

View on Amazon

Specs in Plain English

  • Blade: 3.35 inches, D2 steel, 59 to 61 HRC, flat ground, clip point, black DLC finish
  • Overall length: just under 8 inches open, 4.6 inches closed
  • Blade stock: 0.12 inch, right where a working folder should be
  • Handle: G10 scales over black stainless liners, 0.47 inch thick
  • Lock: liner lock
  • Pivot: caged ceramic ball bearings
  • Deployment: flipper tab and ambidextrous thumb studs
  • Clip: deep carry, tip up, reversible for left or right
  • Weight: 3.59 ounces

For size, this thing sits in Paramilitary 2 territory. The PM2 beats it by maybe a quarter to three eighths of an inch on the blade and handle, but pick them both up and they feel like the same class of knife. It’s noticeably bigger than a Bugout.

Out of the Box

Sharp enough. Not wicked sharp, not the kind of edge that makes you nervous to check it with your thumb, but a decent working edge that cut everything I asked it to. I’ll take decent at this price. Plenty of forty dollar knives show up needing a trip to the stones before you can use them, and this one didn’t.

In the Hand

The G10 has horizontal milled lines in it, which normally makes me suspicious. Horizontal texturing looks aggressive in photos and then slides around in your palm when your hands are wet. This one grips fine. It won’t shred your pocket, it won’t slip. Fine is the word for a lot of this knife, and I mean that as a description, not an insult.

The part I do love is the choil. There’s a finger choil at the base of the blade, and choking up on it puts your index finger right behind the edge with the jimping on the spine under your thumb. That’s my grip for detail work, for cutting tape off a box without cutting the box, for anything where you want control instead of leverage. A lot of knives in this price range skip the choil or get it wrong. SENCUT got it right, and it’s the one detail on this knife that shows somebody cared.

Open construction with standoffs, so it rinses clean. At 3.59 ounces it’s not light, but it’s a full size knife with steel liners and it carries like one. You know it’s there. You don’t resent it.

Action and Lock

The action is fine. That’s the honest word again. Caged ceramic bearings, the flipper gets the blade out, the thumb studs get the blade out, the detent is reasonable, the liner lock engages with very little play. It’s not the buttery, addictive fidget action you get on a CIVIVI at twice the price, and it’s not supposed to be. It opens and it locks and it closes. Two months in, that has not changed.

One small design choice worth pointing out: the thumb studs sit up and out of the sharpening path. Anybody who has tried to sharpen a knife with thumb studs parked right at the heel of the edge knows why that matters.

Blade and Steel

D2 is a known quantity. It holds an edge well, it’s a little more work to sharpen than the softer budget stainless steels, and it’s semi stainless, which means it can spot if you put it away wet and forget about it. Living near salt water, I care about that. The DLC coating on mine has held up clean through a beach trip and a college move, and whatever wear it picks up over time I’ll take as a badge. A knife that looks used is a knife that got used.

The flat grind and 0.12 inch stock make this a slicer with enough spine for the light prying you shouldn’t be doing anyway. The clip point gives you a fine tip for detail work. Cutting edge comes in around three and a quarter inches.

View on Amazon

The Clip

Deep carry, reversible, stainless. A sliver of the handle still peeks out above the seam, so it’s not fully buried, and retention is on the lighter side. It’s not going anywhere, and a lighter clip is easier on your pants and easier to draw. I’ll take it. I’ve torn up enough pockets with clips built like bench vises.

Where It Sits at This Price

This is the crowded end of the pool, so let’s name names.

  • CIVIVI Elementum in D2, around fifty dollars. Slimmer, lighter, more refined, better action. The Sylor is the bigger, grippier, more work ready knife.
  • Spyderco Tenacious, around sixty dollars. Same size class, 8Cr13MoV steel, which is a step down from D2. Spyderco name, four position clip, a little more knife in the pocket.
  • Kershaw Leek, around sixty to seventy dollars. Thinner and dressier, assisted opening, a much more delicate tip. Different job.
  • Benchmade Bugout, around a hundred and fifty dollars. Lighter, better steel, Benchmade warranty. Also more than three times the price, and I’m not sure it’s three times the knife for most people.

At forty to forty six bucks the Sylor isn’t underpriced. It’s priced right, and right in line with everything else at this tier. That’s what people miss when they call SENCUT boring. Ten years ago this knife would have cost ninety dollars. Today it’s the going rate for a well made D2 liner lock. The floor moved up, and SENCUT is standing on it.

Quirks and Complaints

I tried to find something to roast. I really did.

The clip could sit a hair deeper. Retention could be a touch stronger. The edge was decent instead of great. D2 needs a wipe down if you live near salt water. That’s the list. None of those are reasons not to buy it, and none of them surprised me.

Verdict: Should You Buy the SENCUT Sylor?

Yes. If you want a full size, dependable, no drama liner lock for forty bucks, buy it and stop thinking about it.

It’s not flashy. It’s not going to blow you away. It’s a solid, nothing special pocket knife that does the job and gets out of the way, and that’s the whole point of a tool. We’re not cavemen. You buy a thing to make the job easier, and this one does.

Who it’s for: anyone who wants a real working folder without a real working folder’s price. First knife guys. Guys who lose knives. Guys who want a beater that isn’t junk. A great glovebox or truck kit knife.

Who should skip it: if you want something slim and light, look at the Elementum. If you want better steel and a story behind the knife, you already know the names, and you know what they cost.

Fifteen years ago I carried a thirty dollar Walmart Gerber and thought it was the greatest knife ever made. I still own it. It was cheap steel with a sloppy lock, and I loved it anyway. The guy buying that knife today can buy a Sylor for ten dollars more and get bearings, D2, real G10, a choil, and a lock that doesn’t wiggle. That’s a good time to be alive if you like knives.

Just another well built SENCUT. Yep. That’s the review.
